central_concept: regression as a method for studying relationships between a variable of interest and explanatory variables
actuarial_application: framing regression as the dominant statistical method underlying actuarial/financial risk modeling
takeaway: Regression quantifies how a response is explained by other measured variables, illustrated first by Galton's height data.

section_title: Fitting Data to a Normal Distribution
central_concept: using the normal curve to summarize a distribution with two parameters
example_dataset: Massachusetts Automobile Bodily Injury Claims (Rempala and Derrig, 2005)
transformation_used: logarithmic (claims already given in logs of thousands of dollars)
actuarial_application: summarizing insurance claim severity distributions for pricing/reserving
takeaway: Two parameters, mu and sigma^2, can approximate an entire claims distribution via the normal curve.
source_id: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

central_concept: Box-Cox family of power transforms used to symmetrize skewed data
key_formula: y^(lambda) = (y^lambda - 1)/lambda for lambda != 0; ln(y) for lambda = 0
example_dataset: simulated 500 chi-square(2) observations; MA bodily injury claims in dollars
transformation_used: square root, logarithmic, and negative reciprocal transforms (lambda = 1/2, 0, -1)
actuarial_application: many insurance claims distributions are right-skewed and benefit from log transforms before regression
skewness_direction: right-skewed (raw); best symmetrized by log transform
takeaway: The logarithmic transform (lambda=0) is a special case of the Box-Cox family and typically best symmetrizes right-skewed insurance data.
source_id: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

section_title: Sampling and the Role of Normality
central_concept: formal sampling assumptions underlying statistical inference
key_definition: statistic; sampling/data-generating process; the four Basic Sampling Assumptions
statistical_measure: mean ybar and variance s_y^2 used to infer population mu, sigma^2
actuarial_application: justifies statistical inference procedures (e.g., t-statistics) used in actuarial estimation
takeaway: Normality is only one of four sampling assumptions, and is not required for many inference procedures because of central limit theorems.
source_id: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

central_concept: distinguishing designed (experimental) studies from observational studies
key_definition: dependent/explanatory variable terminology; experimental data; observational data; confounding variable
example_dataset: RAND Health Insurance Experiment (Manning et al., 1987); Galton parent-child height data
statistical_measure: statistical control for confounders (e.g., family diet)
actuarial_application: actuarial/social-science data are almost always observational, so causal inference requires statistical rather than experimental control
takeaway: Because actuarial data are observational rather than designed, regression is used for statistical control rather than establishing causality.
source_id: Regression Modeling with Actuarial and Financial Applications_013 - 1.tex

central_concept: the traditional actuarial triad (pricing, reserving, solvency testing) as regression applications
example_dataset: private passenger automobile insurance pricing by sex, age, location, vehicle purpose
actuarial_application: pricing (classification/adverse selection), reserving, and solvency testing
takeaway: Flat-rate pricing that ignores explanatory variables invites adverse selection, which regression-based classification corrects.

central_concept: formal Central Limit Theorem and the Edgeworth approximation for skewness correction
sample_size: n=25 to 50 cited as adequate in practice
statistical_measure: rescaled sample mean ybar approaching standard normal
actuarial_application: justifies approximate normality of regression coefficients, which are weighted averages
skewness_direction: Edgeworth term explicitly corrects for skewness E(ybar-mu)^3
takeaway: The CLT justifies normal approximations for weighted averages like regression coefficients even when raw data are not normal.
